INTRODUCTION 
1. 
By this Order, the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) denies the Office of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia’s (“OPC” 
or “Office”) Application for Reconsideration of Order No. 22860. The Parties are directed to file 
legal briefs in response to Paragraph 84 within twenty (20) days of the date of this Order. 
II.

2. 
On April 13, 2023, the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or the 
“Company”) filed an application for approval to increase rates through the implementation of a 
Multiyear Rate Plan (“MRP”), also referred to as the “Climate Ready Pathway,” for its electric 
distribution service in the District of Columbia (“Pepco Application”) for the years 2024 
through 2026.1 By Order No. 22328, the Commission approved a Formal Case No. 1176 Modified 
MRP Extended Pilot, which authorized Pepco to increase its electric distribution rates during a 
two-year term with a revenue requirement of $99.7 million in 2025 and $23.7 million in 2026 for 
a cumulative revenue requirement increase of $123.4 million over two years.2 
3.

and Office Building Association of Metropolitan Washington (“AOBA”) and OPC of Order 
No. 22328.3 On March 18 and 28, 2025, OPC and AOBA, respectively, petitioned for review of 
Order Nos. 22328 and 22358 to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals (“Court”). 
4.

the Commission had failed to conduct an evidentiary hearing and had not sufficiently explained its 
reasoning on two issues. The Court remanded the matter for further proceedings, including a hearing

III. 
DISCUSSION 
11. 
OPC Application for Reconsideration. According to OPC, the Court vacated the 
entire MRP because there were no factual findings capable of supporting the rate order; therefore, 
no portion of the MRP can lawfully remain in effect.27 OPC argues that vacatur has the legal effect 
of rendering an order null and void, ab initio, meaning it is treated as though it “never occurred” 
and “wipes the slate clean.” Thus, once the Court vacated Order Nos. 22328 and 22358, those 
orders and the entire MRP they approved legally ceased to exist. OPC contends that despite 
acknowledging the vacatur, the Commission incorrectly asserts that the Court did not vacate the 
entire MRP and that the procedural basis for the Court’s decision changes the legal impact of 
vacatur. OPC maintains that both conclusions constitute legal error.28 

12. 
OPC argues that because the Commission never made any factual findings at an 
evidentiary hearing, the entire MRP is invalid, and the issues the Court referenced in its opinion 
were merely illustrative examples, not an exhaustive list of deficiencies.29 OPC contends that the 
Commission misreads the Vacatur Decision by treating only certain components of the MRP, such 
as the Bill Stabilization Adjustment (“BSA”), Effective Rate Adjustment (“ERA”), or explicitly 
noted disputed facts, as vacated, when the Court’s findings of statutory due process violations and 
the absence of any evidentiary record necessarily render the entire rate order and MRP null and 
void.30 

13.

legal text uses terms in their ordinary meaning, and when a statute or judicial opinion uses the 
word “include” before listing examples, the listed items are understood to be illustrative rather

determination on the justness or reasonableness of Pepco’s rates. It was a procedural step designed 
to preserve stability while the Commission conducts the evidentiary hearing required by the Court 
and develops the full record necessary to address all prudency, cost‑variance, and rate‑design 
issues, including any claims related to changed economic conditions.212 In this manner, the remand 
process ensures that concerns about current market conditions are evaluated on the basis of a 
complete evidentiary record and resolved through a merits‑based determination supported by 
substantial evidence. Because the interim rate posture does not foreclose any party’s ability to raise 
or litigate such issues on remand, and because OPC’s economic‑conditions theory does not identify 
an error in the Commission’s prior order, these arguments do not provide a basis for 
reconsideration. 

13. OPC’s Newly Raised Concerns Regarding Customer Mobility and Refund 
Administration Do Not Support Reconsideration 

80. 
OPC additionally argues that the transient nature of many District ratepayers and 
the practical challenges associated with tracking and issuing refunds strengthen the need for 
immediate retroactive relief. These concerns were not raised prior to OPC’s Application for 
Reconsideration, and accordingly, Order No. 22860 did not address this issue. The Commission 
recognizes the importance of ensuring that any remedies ultimately adopted in this proceeding are 
administratively workable and fairly applied to all affected customers, including those who may 
relocate during the pendency of the remand. However, the legal predicate for refunds remains 
unchanged. Under long‑standing District precedent, refunds may be ordered only when the 
underlying rates have been found substantively unlawful; here, the Court identified a procedural 
deficiency but made no determination that the existing rates are unjust, unreasonable, or otherwise 
invalid. Because no such finding has been made, the question of refund administration does not 
arise at this stage. Concerns regarding customer mobility and refund logistics, while important to 
consider in appropriate circumstances, do not establish any error in Order No. 22860 and do not 
provide a basis for reconsideration.

Factual Findings Do Not Support Reconsideration 

81. 
OPC further contends that the MRP has become “purely academic” under the 
judicial mootness doctrine, arguing that the issues presented are no longer live and that the 
Commission cannot provide effective relief. This newly expanded mootness theory was not raised 
before OPC’s Application for Reconsideration, and as a result, Order No. 22860 did not address 
this argument. The Commission finds OPC’s mootness theory unpersuasive because the issues 
remain live and the Commission can still provide effective relief through its remand determination. 
The Court did not hold that the issues presented in this proceeding are moot, nor did it direct the 
Commission to dismiss the MRP. To the contrary, the Court remanded the matter for the 
Commission to conduct the evidentiary hearing previously omitted and to provide additional 
explanation of specific determinations. A controversy plainly remains: the justness and 
reasonableness of Pepco’s rates for the remand period must still be adjudicated on a full evidentiary 
record, and the Commission retains the authority to modify those rates based on the outcome of 
that hearing. Moreover, the Commission has already directed Pepco to submit updated actual 
expenditure data for 2024–2025 and supplemental testimony on prudency, cost variances, and 
ERA/BSA mechanics, ensuring that the remand proceeding will produce a current and complete 
evidentiary record capable of supporting effective prospective relief. The judicial mootness 
doctrine does not apply where, as here, meaningful relief remains available, and the Commission 
is engaged in the adjudicatory process required by the Court. 

82. 
OPC additionally argues that the MRP cannot lawfully be adjudicated on remand 
because, in OPC’s view, Order Nos. 22328 and 22358, and the MRP they approved was vacated 
in its entirety, leaving no proper factual findings. OPC asserts that the absence of prior factual 
findings means the Commission “cannot supplement a plan devoid of factual findings” and that, 
because the forecasts underlying Pepco’s original filing have since been overtaken by actuals, the 
core justiciable issues are now obsolete. The Commission finds OPC’s argument unpersuasive and 
inconsistent with both the Vacatur Decision and the governing statutory framework. First, the 
Court did not hold that the absence of prior factual findings renders the MRP incapable of 
adjudication, nor did it direct the Commission to dismiss the MRP Application. Instead, the Court 
expressly remanded the matter for the Commission to conduct the evidentiary hearing and to 
provide a fuller explanation of specific determinations. A remand to conduct an evidentiary 
hearing necessarily presumes that the Commission must now create the evidentiary record that was 
previously lacking, including making the factual findings required to support whatever rate 
determinations are ultimately made. The absence of prior factual findings is precisely the 
procedural defect the remand is designed to cure, not a basis for dismissal. Second, OPC’s assertion 
that the MRP cannot be supplemented because its forecasts have grown stale misstates both the 
purpose and operation of a remand. As Order No. 22860 explained, the Court did not invalidate 
the MRP framework. Consistent with the remand directive, the Commission has required Pepco to 
file updated actual expenditure data for 2024–2025, along with supplemental testimony addressing 
prudency, cost variances, and the mechanics of the ERA and BSA. These updated data will enable 
the Commission to rebuild the evidentiary record using verified information, ensuring that any 
prospective rate determination rests on substantial, current evidence. The rule against retroactive 
ratemaking does not bar the use of updated actuals to inform prospective ratemaking; it merely 
prohibits retroactive adjustment of previously collected revenues. Third, OPC’s argument that the

not hold that passage of time moots a rate application on remand. Nor does the D.C. Code forbid 
the Commission from adjudicating a partially elapsed multiyear plan where the evidentiary record 
is reconstructed using verified, updated information. The Commission’s process of requiring

83. 
After careful review of OPC’s Application for Reconsideration, the Commission 
finds that OPC has not demonstrated any error of law or fact in Order No. 22860, nor has it 
identified any circumstance warranting the extraordinary remedy of reconsideration. The majority 
of OPC’s arguments repeat positions the Commission has previously considered and rejected. The 
Vacatur Decision was expressly procedural and did not invalidate the MRP framework, the 
existing tariffed rates, or the Commission’s authority to maintain those rates during remand. The 
Court did not order reinstatement of prior rates, mandate refunds, or otherwise disturb the 
Commission’s ratemaking responsibilities. The Commission has already taken significant steps to 
implement the Court’s directive by requiring updated actuals, supplemental testimony, and a full 
evidentiary hearing capable of producing the complete factual record the Court found lacking. The 
Commission remains mindful of its statutory obligations to ensure just and reasonable rates, to 
consider the economic realities faced by District residents, and to maintain transparency and 
fairness throughout the remand proceeding. Nothing in OPC’s Application undermines the 
Commission’s conclusions in Order No. 22860 or the remand process now underway. 
Accordingly, and consistent with the governing legal standards, the Commission reaffirms its 
determinations in Order No. 22860 and denies OPC’s Application for Reconsideration.
